title: Hither! Hither!
text:
“The fool doth think he is wise, but the wise man knows himself to be a fool”

Shenanigans aside, this should serve to elucidate the purpose of this website. Perhaps, in a sense, the world was too boring. And I, being a member of said world, am also boring.





I get bored. Too bored. I need things to occupy my time. I also need a way of “focusing” my projects. It would seem my mind is a zero, containing all things — but mostly no things at all!
Aye, that reminds me. Some time ago when I was pondering. Everything? Nothing? Who knows. Suddenly, a stroke of genius hit me! Yet, I was so lost in (no) thought that I did not even here. Until said thought began screaming — O so loud! And I turned to myself and said “Etc, etc, etc” or however it went. The point being is that I would like to document stray thoughts. They escape me otherwise.
Also, I would like to more fully develop those “stray thoughts” into “stray projects”(?) But, I am thinking to make this more of an informal explanation of tips and tricks that I have come across.
Ah! To resist the urge to demonstrate… Should I? A little example would not hurt. No, it would not hurt at all.

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(2024)
countries <- c("Julia", "Bethania", "Stalwarland")
years <- 2015:2024
panel <- expand.grid(countries = countries,
            years = years)
## seting the stage ----
panel <- panel |> 
  mutate(gdp = NA) 
for(c in countries){ ## yes, I know that there is a better way
  base <- runif(1, 500, 1000)
  growth_rates <- runif(length(years), -0.03, 0.08)
  gdp_path <- base * cumprod(1 + growth_rates)
  panel$gdp[panel$countries == c] <- gdp_path
}
panel <- panel |> 
  mutate(investment = gdp * runif(nrow(panel), 0.15, 0.25))
comp_panel <- panel ## for comparisons sake

The following cell will be transforming panel. Keep that in mind.

for(c in countries){
  for(n in 1:length(panel$gdp[panel$countries == c])){
    if (n == 1){
      panel$gdp_growth[panel$countries == c] <- NA
    }
    else {
      gdp_1 <- panel$gdp[panel$countries == c][n-1]
      gdp_2 <- panel$gdp[panel$countries == c][n]
      panel$gdp_growth[panel$countries == c][n] <- (gdp_2 - gdp_1)/gdp_1
    }
  }
}
panel |> as_tibble() ## again, for comparison's sake

title: Utility and its function
text:
A quick little demonstration of utility functions
We are all well aware of utility functions. So aware that you may question why something like this is even necessary. Many would argue that it is not. But this is primarily to serve as a refresh to myself.
There are some notational things that do require some explanation prior to this refresh, so let’s brush up!

title: Utility and its function
text:
Here we go
Well, let’s get a little bit abstract. Suppose there are two good, x and y that exist on the set of mutually exclusive alternatives. That is to say x, y represent two choices that you can not choose at once. Perhaps you want to go to sleep or go on a run or change your oil or etc. How could you do those simultaneously? The point being is that you can only pick one or the other. This is notationally equivalent to writing \[ x,y \in X  \] Now we can introduce our so-caled (weak) preference relation \(\succsim\). This is a “binary relation on the set of alternatives.” For our purposes, this just means that you can compare each element in the set. If x is weakly preferred to y (x \(\succsim\) y), we can say that “x is at least as good as y.” Awesome.
The one thing about economics that we assume above all else is rationality. So we are going to assume that individual preferences are rational. To assume our assumption we must… make two assumptions about \(\succsim\) : completeness and transitivity.

Completeness: \(\forall x,y \in X\) we have that x \(\succsim\) y or that y \(\succsim\) y or both
Transitvity: \(\forall x,y,z \in X\) we have that if x \(\succsim\) y and y \(\succsim\) z, then x \(\succsim\) z

This is fairly cool, I would say. Our consumer (by property of completenss) has a ranking of elements within the set, and (by property of transitivity) the ranking is consistent.
This is kind of a strong assumption, however. Imagine you, yourself were in a situation where… let’s say you are at Home Depot picking out a color for your kitchen. There are so many colors, so many choices! How can you look at them all and estalish a ranking? Ah! But our individual consumer would have no problem. They would be able to walk into Home Depot, look at all the color opitons, rank them all, and have those rankings be consistent. That is far, far easier said than done.
Again, aside, etc. That should be the bare minimum necessary to go over utility functions.

title: Utility and its function
text:
Utility functions!
A utility function is something a bit abstract, but not to hard to wrap your mind around. The utility function maps each element from the set of alternatives onto the set of real numbers. This allows us to rank othe elements in accordance to the individuals preference.
\[u:X \mapsto  \mathbb{R}\] is a function representing preference relation \(\succsim\) if for all x, y \(\in\) X \[ x \succsim y \iff u(x) \ge u(y)\] As you will soon come to know, a utility function that represents a preference relation \(\succsim\) is not unique. For any strictly increasing function \(f: \mathbb{R} \mapsto  \mathbb{R}\), v(x) = f(u(x)). As long as the ranking of the alternatives is preserved, the utility function is valid!

## for our purposes, we will make x weakly preferred to y
u_x <-  function(x){
  x <- sample(5:10, 1)
}

u_y <-  function(y){
  y <-  sample(1:5, 1)
}

## our strictly increasing function
f <- function(u){
  result <- function(x){
    x * 2
  }
  result
}
## should preserve the order
v_x <- f(u_x)
v_y <- f(u_y)

my_tibble <-  tibble::tribble( 
  ~x, ~y, ~preference,
  "Cats", "Dogs", "x preffered to y",
  "Bats", "Frogs", "x preffered to y",
  "Hats", "Logs", "x preferred to y"
)
my_tibble <- my_tibble |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    u_x = u_x(x), u_y = u_y(y),
    u_great = u_x > u_y,
    v_x = v_x(u_x), v_y = v_y(u_y),
    v_great = v_x > v_y)

my_tibble ## you can see that the order is preserved 

# A tibble: 3 × 9
  x     y     preference         u_x   u_y u_great   v_x   v_y v_great
  <chr> <chr> <chr>            <int> <int> <lgl>   <dbl> <dbl> <lgl>  
1 Cats  Dogs  x preffered to y     6     3 TRUE       12     6 TRUE   
2 Bats  Frogs x preffered to y     6     3 TRUE       12     6 TRUE   
3 Hats  Logs  x preferred to y     6     3 TRUE       12     6 TRUE   


Yes, if you are wondering, I just wanted to show that R is capable of making funciton factories. That was the primary motivatoin in writing this. Putting that aside, let’s prove what that code is showing.

title: Utility and its function
text:
Proof
if \(f: \mathbb{R} \mapsto  \mathbb{R}\), and u:X \(\mapsto  \mathbb{R}\) is a utility function representing preference relation \(\succsim\), then the function v:X \(\mapsto  \mathbb{R}\) defined by v(x) = f(u(x)) is also a utility function representing preference relation \(\succsim\).
We can prove this directly. Assume that f is a strictly increasing function and u(x) is a utility function representing preference relation.
By definition of strictly increasing, we know that for any \(x_2 > x_1\) that \(f(x_2) > f(x_1)\)
By definition of a utility function representing preference relation, we know that \(x \succsim y \iff u(x) \ge u(y)\).
Observe: Consider the utility function u (by our assumption) \[ x \succsim y \iff u(x) \ge u(y)\] We define v(x) as f(u(x)). And since f is a strictly increasing funcion denoted by \[ x_2 > x_1 \iff f(x_2) > f(x_1) \] which by contrapositive is logically equivalent to \[ x_1 \ge x_2 \iff f(x_1) \ge f(x_2)\] Since in our utility function we have u(x) \(\ge\) u(y), we can then say that f(u(x)) \(\ge\) f(u(y)), which is equivalent to: \[ u(x) \ge u(y) \iff v(x) \ge v(y)\] By definition of v(x) = f(u(x))! Thus we can say \[ x \succsim y \iff u(x) \ge u(y) \iff v(x) \ge v(y) \] which means \[ x \succsim y \iff v(x) \ge v(y) \] Thus v is a utility function representing preference relation!
